To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a cell-free system was developed that allows the delivery of influenza viral glycoprotein to the plasma membrane.

the fusion of influenza virus-infected cell vesicles with plasma membrane vesicles bearing Semliki Forest glycoproteins leads to the insertion of the virus neuraminidases into the plasma membrane, that this insertion is ATP-dependent and requires the presence of a trypsin-sensitive protein, and that the fusion of vesicles containing influenza virus neuraminidasae is greatly enhanced when the enzyme is concentrated in a compartment that is between the Golgi apparatus and the plasma membrane.
we have reconstituted a specific exocytotic fusion event in a cell-free system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the intracellular transport and sorting of proteins in eukaryotic cells.
the mechanism of vesicle fusion and the role of proteins in this process.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the transport of membrane glycoproteins to the plasma membrane and their insertion into it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fusion of the vesicles is a result of the fusion of the two proteins.
the cell-free system developed in this study provides a means for the study of a specific exocytosis event, the fusion of vesicles containing viral glycoproteins with the plasma membrane.
the cell-free system is a good tool for studying the mechanism of protein transport in the cell.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fusion between the vesicles is mediated by a protein(s) which is present on the viral membrane.
the insertion of a protein into the plasma membrane can occur as a consequence of fusion between a vesicle containing the protein and a membrane containing the appropriate receptor.
we have developed a cell-free assay for a specific exocytotic event and have shown that the process is ATP-dependent and requires the participation of membrane proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a cell-free assay can be used to study the exocytosis of viral glycoproteins.
a cell-free system can be developed to analyze the fusion of vesicles containing viral proteins with the plasma membrane.
the cell-free assay is an effective tool to study the delivery of viral envelope glycoprote- ins to the plasma membrane and that this delivery is mediated by a specific fusion event.
